title: Buthayna Said, When She Saw
intro: Buthayna saw that Jamil's hair was turning grey, the grey dyed red with henna, and told him he had grown old. These lines are his reply. He reminds her of the places where they spent their youth as neighbours, and of the elegant young man he was, then ends with a question: we are the same age, so how did I grow old, and you did not? The early anthologist Ibn Dawud placed the poem in a chapter on lovers who turn away once grey hair appears.

translation: Buthayna said, when she saw
streaks of red in my hair:
1.sharh: The red is henna. Men dyed their grey hair with it, and it turns white hair a reddish orange, so the red streaks told Buthayna that grey had come.

translation: “You've grown old, Jamil, and your youth is gone.”
I said: Buthayna, hush, say no more!
2.sharh: Buthayna speaks first, teasing or taunting him about his age. He cuts her off, calling her by a shortened, affectionate form of her name.

translation: Have you forgotten our days at al-Liwa,
and our days at Dhawi al-Ajfar?
3.sharh: Al-Liwa and Dhawi al-Ajfar are desert places where they spent their early days together. He asks how she can see only his grey and forget all that.

translation: Didn't you see me, once,
in the nights we spent at Dhu Jahwar,
4.sharh: Dhu Jahwar is another place where their people camped. She saw him there when he was young, as the next lines describe.

translation: nights when your people were our neighbours?
Don't you remember? You do, so remember
5.sharh: Their families camped side by side. He asks if she remembers, and answers for her before she can: of course she does.

translation: when I was a supple youth in my first bloom,
trailing my cloak and my wrap behind me,
6.sharh: He paints himself as he was then: a supple, graceful youth, trailing his clothes along the ground with the swagger of a young man sure of himself.

translation: when my locks were black as a raven's wing,
combed with musk and ambergris.
7.sharh: His long hair was jet black and kept with care, combed and scented with the finest perfumes.

translation: Then what you know of changed all that,
the way this cruel age changes all things.
8.sharh: He doesn't name what changed him; he only says she knows it. It may be the passing years, or what he went through for her love.

translation: And you, like the marzuban's pearl,
still keep the water of your youth, unpressed.
9.sharh: He turns to her: she is still like a precious pearl, the kind a Persian lord would wear. “Water” is the glow of youth, as a pearl's lustre is called its water, and time has not pressed it out of her.

translation: We are close in age; our spring camp was one.
So how did I grow old, and you did not?
10.sharh: They are the same age and grew up in the same place, so his question can be read two ways. Either she is still young in his eyes, or he is gently turning her taunt back on her: if I have aged, so have you.

1.1.2.head: بُثَينة
1.1.2.meaning: Buthayna, a woman of Jamil's own tribe. He loved her from his youth, and his poems to her joined her name to his: he is known as Jamil Buthayna.

1.2.3-4.meaning: “Red hair”: grey hair dyed with henna, which turns white hair a reddish orange. The red gives his age away.

2.2.2.meaning: Buthayn: her name with its last sound dropped. Arabic does this when calling someone close, much like a pet name.

3.1.3.head: اللِّوى
3.1.3.meaning: Al-Liwa: where a sand dune thins out and bends. Here it is the name of a place.

3.2.2-3.head: ذَوو الأَجفَر
3.2.2-3.meaning: Dhawi al-Ajfar: a place in the desert. Ajfar is the plural of jafr, a wide well with unlined sides.

4.2.3-4.head: ذو جَهوَر
4.2.3-4.meaning: Dhu Jahwar: a place named by the early geographer Yaqut, who doesn't say where it was.

5.1.4.meaning: Neighbours. Their families camped next to each other.

6.1.3.meaning: Aghyad: a young man with a soft, swaying neck and a supple build; a picture of youthful grace.

6.2.1.meaning: I trail, I drag. Letting one's clothes sweep the ground was the swagger of a proud, carefree young man.

6.2.2.meaning: Rida': a cloak worn over the shoulders.

6.2.4.meaning: Mi'zar: a wrap tied at the waist. With the rida', it made up a man's dress.

7.1.2.head: اللِّمَّة
7.1.2.meaning: Limma: hair long enough to fall past the earlobes.

7.2.2-3.head: المِسك والعَنبَر
7.2.2-3.meaning: Musk and ambergris: two of the most precious perfumes of the time.

8.2.3-4.meaning: A cruel age: time that does things to people that they can only reject.

9.1.2-3.head: لُؤلُؤة المَرزُبان
9.1.2-3.meaning: The marzuban's pearl. A marzuban was a Persian governor, second only to the king, and such men wore pearls, so his would be among the finest.

9.2.1-2.head: ماء الشباب
9.2.1-2.meaning: “The water of youth”: its freshness and glow. Arabic also calls a pearl's lustre its water.

9.2.4.meaning: Pressed, squeezed: time has not pressed the water of youth out of her.

10.1.2.head: المَربَع
10.1.2.meaning: Marba': the camp where a tribe spends the spring. They grew up in the same place.
